title: Friends across traditions
hookLine: he corresponded with Zen and Jewish teachers and hosted Thich Nhat Hanh

lines: TWO OLD FRIENDS IN A DINER BOOTH.
cards: Two old friends in a diner booth. One prays, one doesn't. They vote differently.

They've argued for years, and they still meet for coffee every month, and each leaves a little larger. Neither has to pretend to agree. Thomas Merton had friendships like that all over the world, in an age of airmail.
A Zen scholar in Japan. A rabbi in New York. A young Vietnamese monk who walked up the road to Gethsemani.

teach.b: First, the letters. From the late 1950s on, Merton wrote to people across many faiths. He corresponded for years with D.
T. Suzuki, the Japanese scholar who brought Zen Buddhism to many English readers, and flew to New York in 1964 to meet him.
He wrote to Abraham Joshua Heschel, the Jewish teacher and theologian; to Louis Massignon, a Catholic scholar of Islam; and to Muslim scholars about Sufi prayer. Second, the visit.
In May 1966, the Vietnamese Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh came to Gethsemani while touring America to speak about the war in his country. The two monks talked for hours.
Afterward Merton published a short piece called Nhat Hanh Is My Brother, asking Americans to listen to him. Third, the Church's own turn.
In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued a short declaration called Nostra Aetate, In Our Time.
It says the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, and it calls Catholics to dialogue with respect. Merton had been living that, one letter at a time.
Paul said it long before, in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good."
Fourth, without erasing. Merton never pretended all traditions were the same, and he never asked anyone to leave their own.

teach.h: HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.
teach.b: He stayed a Catholic monk to the end; his friends stayed Buddhist, Jewish, Muslim. What they shared was honesty, prayer and real curiosity. Friendship didn't flatten the differences.

how: The Catholic Church has official offices for dialogue with other religions, and Catholic monks and nuns, through groups like Monastic Interreligious Dialogue, still meet with Buddhist and other monastics to pray and talk.

games.q: a Vietnamese Buddhist monk visits your monastery, speaking against the war that's tearing his country apart. what do you do?
o: talk for hours, then publicly call him your brother
games.why: Merton and Thich Nhat Hanh talked for hours, and Merton published Nhat Hanh Is My Brother, asking Americans to listen.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose faith, or lack of it, isn't yours, a coworker, a neighbor, a relative, and picture their face kindly. What's one good thing you've seen in them, or one thing they know that you don't?
Be grateful for it without needing to agree about everything; if you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Nostra Aetate, the Second Vatican Council's declaration that the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions, which Merton already lived in friendship. Today's word.
